For the second term in \eqref{eq:overlap-decomposition}, the section bound
above gives
\begin{align}
&\mathbb Q\Big(
 B_r\cap
 \Big\{(u,s):s\leqslant a-\frac{r^2}{16}\Big\}
 \Big)
\leqslant
 C\int_{-\infty}^{a-r^2/16}
 \Big[
 r^d+
 \big(h+\frac{r^2}{256}-s\big)_+^{d/2}
 \Big]\mathbb F(ds).
 \label{eq:overlap-lower-mark-integral}
\end{align}
Since \(a\leqslant z\vee z'\), there exist \(r_0<\infty\) and \(c>0\), such that for \(r\geqslant r_0\),
\(
 s\leqslant a-{r^2}/{16}
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 s_-\geqslant c r^2.
\)
On this integration range, using \(h\leqslant z\), we have
\(
 \Big(h+{r^2}/{256}-s\Big)_+^{d/2}
 \leqslant
 C\Big(r^d+s_-^{d/2}\Big).
\)
Therefore,
\begin{align*}
&\int_{-\infty}^{a-r^2/16}
 \Big[
 r^d+
 \big(h+\frac{r^2}{256}-s\big)_+^{d/2}
 \Big]\mathbb F(ds)
\leqslant
 C r^d\mathbb P(H_-\geqslant c r^2)
 +
 C\mathbb E\left[
 H_-^{d/2}\mathbf{1}\{H_-\geqslant c r^2\}
 \right]
\leqslant
 C r^{-2(q-d/2)}.
\end{align*}
For \(1\leqslant r<r_0\), the same estimate, with a larger constant and with
\((1+r)^{-2\rho}\) on the right-hand side, follows from
\eqref{eq:deterministic-region-measure}. Since
\(q>\rho+d/2\), we have \(2(q-d/2)>2\rho\). Combining the last estimate with
\eqref{eq:overlap-large-cover-time} proves
\eqref{eq:deterministic-overlap-final}.
It remains to prove \eqref{eq:point-hit-final}. On the event
\(\{A_x>0,\ x'\in D_x^V\}\), put
\(
 S_x:=T_x-h\geqslant0,
\) and \(
 \Delta:=(h-h')_+.
\)
The definition of \(D_x^V\) implies
\(
 r
 \leqslant
 \sqrt{S_x}+\sqrt{h+S_x-h'}
 \leqslant
 \sqrt{S_x}+\sqrt{S_x+\Delta}
 \leqslant
 2\sqrt{S_x}+\sqrt\Delta.
\)

Suppose first that \(\sqrt\Delta<r/2\). Then
\(
 2\sqrt{S_x}
 \geqslant
 r-\sqrt\Delta
 >
 \frac r2,
\)
and hence \(S_x>r^2/16\). Corollary~\ref{lem:cover-time-moment-integrability}
and Markov's inequality give
\begin{align}
&\mathbb P\left(
 A_x>0,\ x'\in D_x^V,\ \sqrt\Delta<\frac r2
 \right)
\leqslant
 \mathbb P\left(
 A_x>0,\ S_x>\frac{r^2}{16}
 \right)
 \leqslant
 C\bigl(1+(z-h)_+^m\bigr)r^{-2m}.
 \label{eq:point-hit-large-cover-time}
\end{align}
Since \(m>\rho\) and \(r\geqslant1\), this is bounded by
\(
 C\bigl(1+(z-h)_+^m\bigr)(1+r)^{-2\rho}.
\)
Suppose finally that \(\sqrt\Delta\geqslant r/2\). Then
\(
 h-h'\geqslant\frac{r^2}{4}.
\)
Since \(h\leqslant z\) and \(h'\leqslant z'\), we have
\(
 h-h'
 \leqslant
 z-h'
 \leqslant
 (z'-h')_+ +(z-z')_+.
\)
Thus, there exist \(r_1<\infty\) and \(c_1>0\), depending only on \(z,z'\),
such that for \(r\geqslant r_1\),
\(
 (z'-h')_+\geqslant c_1r^2.
\)
Because \(m>\rho\), we have
\(
 1
 \leqslant
 C\bigl(1+(z'-h')_+^m\bigr)(1+r)^{-2\rho}
\)
on this event. For \(1\leqslant r<r_1\), the same inequality follows after
increasing \(C\), because the mark factors are at least one. Combining this estimate
with \eqref{eq:point-hit-large-cover-time} proves
\eqref{eq:point-hit-final}. Interchanging
\((x,z)\) and \((x',z')\) proves the symmetric estimate.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
In view of Remark \ref{rem:Qlb}, we split $I_\alpha$ as
                                                                                                                      
\begin{align*}
	I_\alpha(x_2) &\leqslant C \int_{\mathbb R^{d+1}}  (1+h_{1,-}^t) \mathbf{1}\left\{a\|v_1 - v_2\|^2+ bh_1+ch_2 \geqslant x_0\right\}\exp\big(-C \big(a\|v_1 - v_2\|^2+ bh_1+ch_2-x_0\big)^{d/2}\big) \mathbb{Q}(dx_1) \\
	& + \int_{\mathbb R^{d+1}} (1+h_{1,-}^t)\mathbf{1}\left\{0 \leqslant a\|v_1 - v_2\|^2 \leqslant x_0 - bh_1 - c h_2 \right\} \mathbb{Q}(dx_1) =: I_1 + I_2.
\end{align*}
	Then using $\mathbb E H_-^{t+d/2}<\infty$ and the change of variables $s := a\|v_1 - v_2\|^2$,
\begin{align*}
	I_1 & \leqslant C \int_{-\infty}^\infty \int_{4x_0}^\infty  (1+h_{1,-}^t) (s-bh_1-ch_2 + x_0)_+^{\frac{d}{2} -1} \exp\big(-C s^{d/2}\big) \, ds \mathbb F(dh_1)\\
	& \leqslant C \int_{-\infty}^\infty \int_{4x_0}^\infty  (1+h_{1,-}^t) (1+ |s|^{\frac{d}{2} -1} +h_{1,-}^{\frac{d}{2} -1} + h_{2,-}^{\frac{d}{2} -1}) \exp\big(-C s^{d/2}\big) \, ds \mathbb F(dh_1) \in  O(h_{2,-}^{d/2-1}),
\end{align*}
while
$
I_2 \leqslant C \int_{-\infty}^\infty  (1+h_{1,-}^t) \big(x_0 - bh_1 - ch_2\big)_+^{d/2} \, \mathbb F(dh_1) \in O(h_{2,-}^{d/2}). 
$
Combining these bounds, we obtain
$I_\alpha(x_2)\in O(h_{2,-}^{d/2})$
for every $t\in[0,(m-1/2)d]$ and $\alpha>0$.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label{lem:qbound}
	Assume $\mathbb E[H_-^{md}]<\infty$.	There exists a constant $c > 0$ such that $q(x_1, x_2)$ satisfies
	\begin{equation*}
		q(x_1, x_2) \lesssim \big( 1 + h_{1,-}^{d/2} + h_{2,-}^{d/2}\big)  \mathbf{1}\{A \leqslant 2x_0\}  + [(1+A)^{-(m-1/2)d} + \exp(-c A^{d/2})] \mathbf{1}\{A >0\}.
	\end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
Recall that $q(x_1, x_2) = \int_{W_n^z} \mathbb{P}(\{x_1, x_2\} \subseteq D^{\mathsf V}(x_3, T_3)) \mathbb Q(d x_3)$, where we write $T_3 \equiv T(x_3, \mathcal{P}+ \delta_{x_3})$ for notational simplicity. As noted in \eqref{eq:tailbd}, for $x_1$ and $x_2$ to be covered, the cover time $T_3$ must satisfy
	\begin{equation*}
		T_3 \geqslant \frac{1}{8}\|v_1-v_3\|^2 + ({h_1 + h_3})/{2} \quad \text{and} \quad T_3 \geqslant \frac{1}{8}\|v_2-v_3\|^2 + (h_2 + h_3)/{2}.
	\end{equation*}
	Since $v_3 \in W_n$, we have $\|v_i-v_3\|^2 \geqslant d(v_i, W_n)^2$ for $i \in \{1, 2\}$. Decompose for $i \in \{1,2\}$,
	\begin{align*}
		\frac{1}{8}\|v_i-v_3\|^2 &\geqslant \frac{1}{16}\|v_i-v_3\|^2 + \frac{1}{32}d(v_i, W_n)^2 + \frac{1}{32}\|v_i-v_3\|^2.
	\end{align*}
	Substituting these into the bounds for $T_3$ and taking their arithmetic mean yields
	\begin{equation*}
		T_3 \geqslant \frac{1}{32}\|v_1-v_3\|^2 + \frac{1}{32}\|v_2-v_3\|^2 + \frac{1}{64}d(v_1, W_n)^2 + \frac{1}{64}d(v_2, W_n)^2 + \frac{1}{64}\|v_1-v_3\|^2 + \frac{1}{64}\|v_2-v_3\|^2 + \frac{h_1+h_2+2h_3}{4}.
	\end{equation*}
	Applying the geometric triangle inequality $\frac{1}{64}\|v_1-v_3\|^2 + \frac{1}{64}\|v_2-v_3\|^2 \geqslant \frac{1}{128}\|v_1-v_2\|^2$, and dropping $\frac{1}{32}\|v_2-v_3\|^2 + \frac{1}{64}d(v_1, W_n)^2\geqslant 0$, we obtain
	\begin{equation*}
		T_3 \geqslant \frac{1}{32}\|v_1-v_3\|^2 + \underbrace{ \frac{1}{128}\|v_1-v_2\|^2                              
			+ \frac{1}{64}d(v_2, W_n)^2 + \frac{h_1+h_2}{4} }_{2 A(x_1, x_2)} + \frac{h_3}{2}.
	\end{equation*}
	Since the event $\{\{x_1, x_2\} \subseteq D^{\mathsf V}(x_3, T_3)\}$ also forces $T_3 >h_3$, using the exponential tail bound in Proposition \ref{prop:CoverTimetail}(iii), we obtain
	\begin{equation*}
		q(x_1, x_2) \leqslant \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d, z}} \exp\big(-\frac{1}{2^d}\mathbb{Q}\big( \frac{1}{64}\|v_1-v_3\|^2 + A(x_1, x_2) + \frac{3h_3}{4} \big)\big) \mathbb Q(dx_3).
	\end{equation*}
	Further denote $K = A(x_1, x_2) + {3h_3}/{4}$. We first evaluate the inner spatial integral over $v_3 \in \mathbb{R}^d$:
	\begin{equation*}
		J(K) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \exp\big(-\frac{1}{2^d}\mathbb{Q}\big(\frac{1}{64}\|v_1-v_3\|^2 + K\big)\big) \,dv_3.
	\end{equation*}
	Applying the substitution $y = (v_1-v_3)/\sqrt{32}$ (which implies $dv_3 \asymp dy$), we partition the integration domain into regions $U_1 = \{ \|y\|^2 + K \leqslant x_0 \}$ and $U_2 = \{ \|y\|^2 + K > x_0 \}$. Integrating over $U_1$ yields
	\begin{equation*}
		\int_{U_1} \exp\big(-\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{Q}(\|y\|^2 + K)\big) \,dy \leqslant \int_{\|y\|^2 \leqslant (x_0 - K)_+} 1 \, dy = \kappa_d (x_0 - K)_+^{d/2}.
	\end{equation*}
	On $U_2$, the argument exceeds $x_0$, so that the polynomial lower bound $\mathbb{Q}(u) \geqslant \tilde{c} u^{d/2}$ applies by Remark \ref{rem:Qlb}.
	\begin{itemize}
		\item \textbf{Case 1 ($K \geqslant 0$):} In this case, we have $K = K_+$ and thus
		\begin{equation*}
			\int_{U_2} \exp\big(-\frac{\tilde{c}}{2}(\|y\|^2 + K)^{d/2}\big) \,dy \leqslant \exp(-c K_+^{d/2}) \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \exp(-c \|y\|^d) dy \lesssim \exp(-c K_+^{d/2}).
		\end{equation*}
		\item \textbf{Case 2 ($K < 0$):} Here we apply the substitution $u = \|y\|^2 + K$. The domain is $u > x_0$, and the radial measure transforms to $dy \propto (u + |K|)^{(d-2)/2} du$. Since $(u+|K|)^{(d-2)/2} \lesssim (u^{(d-2)/2} + |K|^{(d-2)/2})$, integrating against $\exp(-\frac{\tilde{c}}{2}u^{d/2})$ yields
		\(
			\int_{U_2} \exp\big(-\frac{\tilde{c}}{2}u^{d/2}\big) \, dy \lesssim 1+ |K|^{(d-2)/2} \lesssim (x_0 - K)_+^{d/2}.
		\)
	\end{itemize}
	Summing the bounds yields 
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:J}
		J(K) \leqslant C \big( (x_0 - K)_+^{d/2} + \exp(-c K_+^{d/2}) \big).
	\end{equation}
	
	Finally, we integrate $J(K) =J(A(x_1, x_2) + \frac{3h_3}{4})$ over $h_3 \in (-\infty, z]$ with respect to $h_3$ to obtain a bound on $q(x_1,x_2)$. Writing $A\equiv A(x_1,x_2)$, for the first summand in \eqref{eq:J}, we must evaluate the integral
	\begin{equation*}
		I_{cut}(A) := \int_{-\infty}^z \big(x_0 - A - \frac{3h_3}{4}\big)_+^{d/2} \,\mathbb F(dh_3) \leqslant \int_{-\infty}^z \big(x_0 - A + \frac{3}{4}h_{3,-}\big)_+^{d/2} \,\mathbb F(dh_3).
	\end{equation*}
	Note that the integrand is zero unless $\frac{3}{4}h_{3,-} > A - x_0$.
	
	\begin{itemize}
			\item \textbf{Case 1 ($A \leqslant 2x_0$):} 
			Noting $-A \leqslant \frac{1}{8}h_{1,-} + \frac{1}{8}h_{2,-}$ and using subadditivity, we bound the integral
			\begin{align*}
				I_{cut}(A) \mathbf{1}\{A \leqslant 2x_0\} &\leqslant \mathbf{1}\{A \leqslant 2x_0\} \int_{-\infty}^z \big( x_0 + \frac{1}{8}h_{1,-} + \frac{1}{8}h_{2,-} + \frac{3}{4}h_{3,-} \big)^{d/2} \,\mathbb F(dh_3)\\
				&\leqslant C \mathbf{1}\{A \leqslant 2x_0\} \big( 1 + h_{1,-}^{d/2} + h_{2,-}^{d/2}\big).
			\end{align*}
		
		\item \textbf{Case 2 ($A > 2x_0$):} 
		Since $A > 2x_0$, we have $A - x_0 > {A}/{2}$. Thus, the integrand in $I_{cut}(A)$ is non-zero only if $\frac{3}{4}h_{3,-} > {A}/{2}$. On this restricted domain, dropping $x_0 - A \leqslant 0$ term, and integrating yields
		\begin{equation*}
			I_{cut}(A) \mathbf{1}\{A > 2x_0\} \leqslant \int_{-\infty}^{-\frac{2A}{3}} \big( \frac{3}{4}h_{3,-} \big)^{d/2} \mathbb F(dh_3) \leqslant C \min\{\mathbb E H_-^{d/2},A^{-(m-1/2) d} \mathbb E H_-^{m d}\} \in O((1+A)^{-(m-1/2) d}).
		\end{equation*}
	\end{itemize}
	Thus,
	\begin{equation*}
		I_{cut}(A) \leqslant C \big( 1 + h_{1,-}^{d/2} + h_{2,-}^{d/2}\big)\mathbf{1}\{A \leqslant 2x_0\} + C(1+A)^{-(m-1/2) d} \mathbf{1}\{A > 2x_0\}.
	\end{equation*}
	
	Finally, we consider the exponential tail term in \eqref{eq:J}. If $A \leqslant 0$, we  trivially bound the exponential by $1$. If $A > 0$, we partition the integration domain for $h_3$:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item \textbf{Case 1 $\big( 3h_{3,-} \leqslant 2{A} \big)$:} Here, $A + \frac{3h_3}{4} \geqslant {A}/{2}$. The exponential is thus bounded by $\exp(-c (A/2)^{d/2})$. Integrating over $h_3$ thus yields a bound $\exp(-c' A^{d/2})$ for some $c'>0$.
		\item \textbf{Case 2 $\big( {3}h_{3,-} > 2{A} \big)$:} In this case, we bound the exponential term by $1$. By Markov's inequality and our assumed $md$ finite moments for $H_-$,
		\begin{equation*}
			\mathbb{P}\big( H_- > {2A}/{3} \big) \lesssim \min\{1,A^{-m d} \mathbb{E}[H_-^{m d}]\} \lesssim (1+A)^{-md}.
		\end{equation*}
	\end{itemize}
	
	Summing the different bounds and noting $x_0 \geqslant 0$, we obtain
	\begin{align*}
		q(x_1, x_2) &\leqslant C \big( 1 + h_{1,-}^{d/2} + h_{2,-}^{d/2}\big)\mathbf{1}\{A \leqslant 2x_0\} + (1+A)^{-(m-1/2)d} \mathbf{1}\{A > 2x_0\} \\
		& \qquad \qquad + \mathbf{1}\{A \leqslant 0\} + [\exp(-c' A^{d/2}) + (1+A)^{-md}]\mathbf{1}\{A >0\} \\
		& \leqslant C  \big( 1 + h_{1,-}^{d/2} + h_{2,-}^{d/2}\big)\mathbf{1}\{A \leqslant 2x_0\}  + [(1+A)^{-(m-1/2) d} + \exp(-c' A^{d/2})] \mathbf{1}\{A >0\},
	\end{align*}
	completing the proof.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
Recall that
$
	f_\alpha^{(3)}(x_2) \lesssim \int_{\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb R}S(x_1) q(x_1, x_2)^\alpha \, dv_1 \mathbb F(dh_1),
	$
where $S(x_1) \in O( (h_{1,-}^{5d/2}))$. For the application of Theorem \ref{thm:KolBd}, it is enough to prove
\[
\mathbb Q\big((f_\tau^{(3)})^2\big)\in O(|W_n|)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\mathbb Q f_{2\tau}^{(3)}\in O(|W_n|),
\]
where
$\tau=3/20$. For $x_i=(v_i,h_i)$, $i=1,2$, put
\(
B:=c_0\|v_1-v_2\|^2+D,
\)
\(c_0:=\frac1{256},
\) and \(
D:=\frac1{128}d(v_2,W_n)^2,
\)
and
\(
H:=\frac18h_{1,-}+\frac18h_{2,-}.
\)
By the definition \eqref{def:A},
\(
A(x_1,x_2)
=
B+\frac{h_1+h_2}{8}
\geqslant B-H.
\)



For $\alpha\in[\tau,2\tau]$, by Lemma \ref{lem:qbound} and using subadditivity of $x\mapsto x^\alpha$, we can bound
\begin{align}\label{eq:qbd}
	q(x_1, x_2)^\alpha &\leqslant \left[ \big(1 + h_{1,-}^{\frac{d\alpha}{2}} + h_{2,-}^{\frac{d\alpha}{2}}\big)\mathbf{1}\{A \leqslant 2x_0\}  + (1+A)^{-\lambda_\alpha} \mathbf{1}\{A > 0\} + \exp(-c\alpha A^{d/2}) \mathbf{1}\{A > 0\} \right],
\end{align}
where we write $\lambda_\alpha:=(m-\tfrac12)d\alpha$. Since $m>11/2$ and $\alpha\geqslant\tau=3/20$, note that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:lambda-lower-V}
	\lambda_\alpha
	\geqslant (m-\tfrac12)d\tau
	>5d\frac{3}{20}
	=\frac{3d}{4} >\frac{d}{2}.
\end{equation}

We now bound the contributions in \eqref{eq:qbd} separately. For the first term, note that since $A\geqslant B-H$, we have $A\leqslant2x_0 \implies
B\leqslant H+2x_0$.
Since $x_0\geqslant0$ is fixed, this implies
\(
\mathbf{1}\{A\leqslant2x_0\}
\lesssim
{(1+H)^{\lambda_\alpha}}/
{(1+B)^{\lambda_\alpha}}.
\)
Consequently,
\begin{align}\label{eq:q-small-A-V}
	\big(
	1+h_{1,-}^{d\alpha/2}
	+h_{2,-}^{d\alpha/2}
	\big)\mathbf{1}\{A\leqslant2x_0\}
	&\lesssim
	\frac{
		\big(
		1+h_{1,-}^{d\alpha/2}
		+h_{2,-}^{d\alpha/2}
		\big)
		(1+H)^{\lambda_\alpha}}
	{(1+B)^{\lambda_\alpha}} \nonumber\\
	&\lesssim
	\frac{
		1+h_{1,-}^{\lambda_\alpha+d\alpha/2}
		+h_{2,-}^{\lambda_\alpha+d\alpha/2}}
	{(1+B)^{\lambda_\alpha}} = \frac{
		1+h_{1,-}^{md\alpha}
		+h_{2,-}^{md\alpha}}
	{(1+B)^{\lambda_\alpha}}.
\end{align}


Next, on $\{A>0\}$, using $A\geqslant B-H$ gives
\(
1+A
\geqslant
1+(B-H)_+.
\)
Note the elementary inequality
\(
	\big(1+(t-s)_+\big)^{-\lambda}
	\leqslant
	(1+s)^\lambda(1+t)^{-\lambda}\) for \(
	s,t\geqslant0, \lambda>0.
	\)
Indeed,
\(
1+t
\leqslant
(1+s)\big(1+(t-s)_+\big),
\)
which immediately yields the above inequality.
Using this, we obtain
\begin{align}
	(1+A)^{-\lambda_\alpha}\mathbf{1}\{A>0\}
	&\leqslant
	\big(1+(B-H)_+\big)^{-\lambda_\alpha}
\leqslant
	\frac{(1+H)^{\lambda_\alpha}}
	{(1+B)^{\lambda_\alpha}} \lesssim
	\frac{
		1+h_{1,-}^{md\alpha}
		+h_{2,-}^{md\alpha}}
	{(1+B)^{\lambda_\alpha}}.
	\label{eq:q-poly-A-V}
\end{align}

Finally, since $\alpha\in[\tau,2\tau]$ is bounded away from zero and
$\lambda_\alpha$ ranges over a bounded interval, there exists
$C<\infty$, uniformly in $\alpha\in[\tau,2\tau]$, such that
\(
e^{-c\alpha u^{d/2}} 
\leqslant
C(1+u)^{-\lambda_\alpha},
\)
for  \(u\geqslant0\).
Together with \eqref{eq:q-poly-A-V}, this yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:q-exp-A-V}
	e^{-c\alpha A^{d/2}}\mathbf{1}\{A>0\} \lesssim (1+A)^{-\lambda_\alpha}\mathbf{1}\{A>0\} 
	\lesssim
	\frac{
		1+h_{1,-}^{md\alpha}
		+h_{2,-}^{md\alpha}}
	{(1+B)^{\lambda_\alpha}}.
\end{equation}

Combining \eqref{eq:q-small-A-V}, \eqref{eq:q-poly-A-V} and
\eqref{eq:q-exp-A-V} via \eqref{eq:qbd}, we arrive at the uniform bound
\begin{equation}\label{eq:qalphaV}
	q(x_1,x_2)^\alpha
	\lesssim
	\frac{
		1+h_{1,-}^{md\alpha}
		+h_{2,-}^{md\alpha}}
	{\big(
		1+c_0\|v_1-v_2\|^2+D
		\big)^{\lambda_\alpha}},
	\qquad
	\alpha\in[\tau,2\tau].
\end{equation}


We next integrate with respect to $v_1$. The change of variables
\(
v_1-v_2=\sqrt{1+D}\,y
\)
gives
\begin{align}
	&\int_{\mathbb R^d}
	\big(
	1+c_0\|v_1-v_2\|^2+D
	\big)^{-\lambda_\alpha}
	\,dv_1
	=
	(1+D)^{d/2-\lambda_\alpha}
	\int_{\mathbb R^d}
	\big(1+c_0\|y\|^2\big)^{-\lambda_\alpha}
	\,dy \lesssim
	(1+D)^{-(\lambda_\alpha-d/2)},
	\label{eq:spatial-qalpha-V}
\end{align}
where the final step follows upon noting that $\lambda_\alpha>d/2$ by \eqref{eq:lambda-lower-V}. Using \eqref{eq:qalphaV}, \eqref{eq:spatial-qalpha-V} and
$S(x_1)\lesssim1+h_{1,-}^{5d/2}$, we therefore obtain
\begin{align*}
	f_\alpha^{(3)}(x_2)
	&\lesssim
	\frac{1}{(1+D)^{\lambda_\alpha-d/2}}
	\int_{\mathbb R}
	(1+h_{1,-}^{5d/2})
	\big(
	1+h_{1,-}^{md\alpha}
	+h_{2,-}^{md\alpha}
	\big)
	\mathbb F(dh_1).
\end{align*}
Since
\(
\frac52+m\alpha
\leqslant
\frac52+\frac{3m}{10}
<m,
\)
for $\alpha\in[\tau,2\tau]$, with the final inequality following from $m>11/2$, the assumed condition $\mathbb E H_-^{md}<\infty$ thus implies
   
                 
                   
                       
                
   
              
\begin{equation}\label{eq:f3-pointwise-V}
	f_\alpha^{(3)}(x_2)
	\lesssim
	\frac{1+h_{2,-}^{md\alpha}}
	{(1+D)^{\lambda_\alpha-d/2}},
	\qquad
	\alpha\in[\tau,2\tau].
\end{equation}

Now let $\alpha=2\tau=3/10$. 
From \eqref{eq:f3-pointwise-V}, we have
\(
f_{2\tau}^{(3)}(x_2)
\lesssim
{1+h_{2,-}^{2md\tau}}/
{(1+D)^{\lambda_{2\tau}-d/2}}.
\)
For $v_2\in W_{2n}^c$, we have
\(
d(v_2,W_n)\geqslant c_W\|v_2\|
\)
for some $c_W>0$, and hence
\(
D\gtrsim\|v_2\|^2.
\)
Noting
\(
2m\tau=\frac{3m}{10}<m,
\)
so the $h_2$-integral is finite, we obtain
\begin{align*}
\mathbb Q f_{2\tau}^{(3)} &\lesssim \int_{\mathbb R}
(1+h_{2,-}^{2md\tau} )
\,\mathbb{F}(dh_2) \left(|W_{2n}|	+ \int_{W_{2n}^c}
	(1+D)^{-(\lambda_{2\tau}-d/2)}
	\,dv_2 \right)
	&\lesssim |W_n| +
	\int_{\mathbb R^d}
	(1+\|v\|^2)^{-(\lambda_{2\tau}-d/2)}
	\,dv.
\end{align*}
The integral above is finite since noting that $m>11/2$, we have
\(
\lambda_{2\tau}
=
(m-\tfrac12)d\frac{3}{10}
>
\frac{3d}{2}
>d.
\)
Therefore,
\(
\mathbb Q f_{2\tau}^{(3)}\in O(|W_n|)
\)
proving the first bound in \eqref{eq:f3bds}.



Finally for $\alpha=\tau=3/20$, we have
\(
\lambda_\tau
=
(m-\tfrac12)d\frac{3}{20}
>
\frac{3d}{4},
\)
because $m>11/2$. Squaring \eqref{eq:f3-pointwise-V} gives
\(
\big(f_\tau^{(3)}(x_2)\big)^2
\lesssim
{1+h_{2,-}^{2md\tau}}/
{(1+D)^{2(\lambda_\tau-d/2)}}.
\)
Since
\(
2m\tau
=
\frac{3m}{10}
<m\), arguing as above yields
\begin{align*}
	\mathbb Q\big((f_\tau^{(3)})^2\big) &\lesssim \int_{\mathbb R}
	(1+h_{2,-}^{2md\tau} )
	\,\mathbb{F}(dh_2) \left(|W_{2n}|	+ \int_{W_{2n}^c}
	(1+D)^{-2(\lambda_\tau-d/2)}
	\,dv_2 \right)\\
	&\lesssim |W_n| +
\int_{\mathbb R^d}
(1+\|v\|^2)^{-2(\lambda_\tau-d/2)}
\,dv.
\end{align*}
The latter integral is again finite since
\(
2(\lambda_\tau-d/2)>\frac d2,
\)
or equivalently
\(
\lambda_\tau>\frac{3d}{4},
\)
which was verified above. Hence,
\(
\mathbb Q\big((f_\tau^{(3)})^2\big)\in O(|W_n|).
\)
This yields the second bound in \eqref{eq:f3bds}, concluding the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:fmombdV}.
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
\label{lem:BM55ext}
For $H$ as in Theorem \ref{thm:KolBd}, assume that conditions {\rm (A1)} and {\rm (A2)} hold. Set
\(
    r_p:=4+p/2
\) and \(
    k_p:=4+\lceil p/2\rceil
\).
Let $g$ and $h$ be defined as in \eqref{eq:g}. Then there exists a constant $C_p\in(0,\infty)$, depending
only on $p$, such that, for every $y\in\mathbb R^{d+1}$ and every
$\mu\in\mathbf N$ with $\mu(\mathbb R^{d+1})\leqslant1$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:BM55ext}
    \mathbb E\big|D_yH(\mathcal P+\mu)\big|^{r_p}
    \leqslant
    C_p\left[
        M_p(y)^{r_p}
        +
        h(y)\big(1+g(y)^{k_p-1}\big)
    \right].
\end{equation}
In particular, with $S$ defined in \eqref{eq:g}, there exists a constant $C_p'\in(0,\infty)$, depending
only on $p$ such that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:BM55extS}
    \mathbb E\big|D_yH(\mathcal P+\mu)\big|^{r_p}
    \leqslant C_p' S(y)^{r_p/4}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
We only indicate the modifications to the proof of
\cite[Lemma 5.5]{BM22}. We first note that the analogue of \cite[Lemma 5.4]{BM22}
continues to hold. Now following the proof of \cite[Lemma 5.5]{BM22}, for $\mu=0$, Lemma 5.2 therein gives
\(
    D_yH(\mathcal P)
    =
    \xi(y;\mathcal P+\delta_y)
    +
    \sum_{x\in\mathcal P}D_y\xi(x;\mathcal P).
\)
By (A2) and monotonicity of $L^q$-norms,
\(
    \mathbb E\big|\xi(y;\mathcal P+\delta_y)\big|^{r_p}
    \leqslant M_p(y)^{r_p}
\). For the second term, arguing as in \cite[Lemma 5.5]{BM22}, one obtains 
\(
    \mathbb E\big|
        \sum_{x\in\mathcal P}D_y\xi(x;\mathcal P)
    \big|^{r_p}
    \leqslant
    C_1\sum_{i=1}^{k_p} I_i,
\)
for some constant $C_1 \in (0,\infty)$ depending only on $p$, where
\[
    I_i
    :=
    \mathbb E
    \sum_{(x_1,\ldots,x_i)\in\mathcal P_{\neq}^i}
    \mathbf{1}\left\{
        D_y\xi(x_j;\mathcal P)\neq0,\ j=1,\ldots,i
    \right\}
    |D_y\xi(x_1;\mathcal P)|^{r_p}.
\]
The only difference from \cite[Lemma 5.5]{BM22} is that the
expansion now contains terms indexed by $i=1,\ldots,k_p$. In the
H\"older step of the proof therein, with $\varepsilon=p/2$, the
probability exponent is
\[
    \frac{p-\varepsilon}{4i+pi}
    =
    \frac{p}{2i(4+p)}
    \geqslant
    \frac{p}{2k_p(4+p)}
    =
    \zeta .
\]
Hence, the same argument gives
\(
    I_i\leqslant C_2 g(y)^{i-1}h(y),
    \;i\leqslant k_p,
\)
and therefore
\(
    \sum_{i=1}^{k_p}I_i
    \leqslant
    C_3 h(y)\bigl(1+g(y)^{k_p-1}\bigr)
\)
for some constants $C_2, C_3 \in (0,\infty)$ depending only on $p$.
This proves \eqref{eq:BM55ext} for $\mu=0$. If $\mu(\mathbb R^{d+1})=1$, the same argument applies with the
additional deterministic point inserted throughout.

It remains to obtain \eqref{eq:BM55extS}. Noting
\(
    k_p-1<r_p,
\)
by the definition of $S$ in \eqref{eq:g}, we have 
\[
    h(y)\big(1+g(y)^{k_p-1}\big)
    \leqslant
    C_4
    \left[
        h(y)^{4/r_p}(1+g(y)^4)
    \right]^{r_p/4} \leqslant C_4 S(y)^{r_p/4}
\]
for some constant $C_4 \in (0,\infty)$ depending only on $p$. Since
\(
    M_p(y)^4\leqslant S(y),
\)
\eqref{eq:BM55extS} now follows from \eqref{eq:BM55ext}.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
We first estimate \(\zeta_2^{(2)}\) and \(\zeta_3^{(2)}\). Fix \(i \in [m]\). We begin with the fourth moment of the iterated add-one cost operator. Write
\[
Y_{i,x,y} := D^{(2)}_{x,y}\hat G_{n,*}(z_i).
\]
Since \(4 < 4+p/2\), the elementary inequality \(\|Y\|_4 \leqslant \|Y\|_{4+p/2} \mathbb P(Y \neq 0)^{1/4-1/(4+p/2)}\) yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Y_norm_step}
\|Y_{i,x,y}\|_4
\leqslant
\|Y_{i,x,y}\|_{4+p/2}\,
\mathbb P\big(Y_{i,x,y} \neq 0\big)^{p/(32+4p)}.
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\(
D^{(2)}_{x,y}F(\mathcal P)
=
D_xF(\mathcal P+\delta_y)-D_xF(\mathcal P),
\)
and hence \(|D^{(2)}_{x,y}F(\mathcal P)| \leqslant |D_xF(\mathcal P+\delta_y)| + |D_xF(\mathcal P)|\). Therefore,
\[
\|Y_{i,x,y}\|_{4+p/2}
\leqslant
2 \max_{u \in \{0,y\}} \big\|D_x\hat G_{n,*}(z_i)(\mathcal P+\delta_u)\big\|_{4+p/2}
\leqslant
2 \max_{u \in \mathbb R^{d+1}} \big\|D_x\hat G_{n,*}(z_i)(\mathcal P+\delta_u)\big\|_{4+p/2}.
\]
Combining this with \eqref{eq:Y_norm_step}, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:D2_basic_bound}
\|D^{(2)}_{x,y}\hat G_{n,*}(z_i)\|_4
\leqslant C
\max_{u \in \mathbb R^{d+1}}
\big\|D_x\hat G_{n,*}(z_i)(\mathcal P+\delta_u)\big\|_{4+p/2}
\,
\mathbb P\big(D^{(2)}_{x,y}\hat G_{n,*}(z_i)\neq 0\big)^\tau,
\end{equation}
where \(\tau := p/(32+4p)\).
Arguing as in \cite[Lemma 5.6]{BM22}, one can bound
$$
\mathbb P \left(D_{x,y}^{(2)} \hat G_{n, *}(z_i) \neq 0\right) \lesssim e^{-r^{(z_i)}(x,y)} + e^{-r^{(z_i)}(y,x)} + q^{(z_i)}(x,y).
$$
On the other hand, by Lemma \ref{lem:BM55ext}, for $i \in [m]$ and $x=(v,h)$
\begin{align*}
&|W_n|^{\frac{4+p/2}{2}} \max_{u \in \mathbb R^{d+1}} \mathbb E \left|D_x \hat G_{n, *}(z_i) (\mathcal{P} + \delta_u)\right|^{4+p/2} \lesssim                                                                    
\left(S^{(z_i)}(x)\right)^{\frac{4+p/2}{4}}.
\end{align*}
Combining the bounds then yields
$$
\left(\mathbb{E}\left(D_{x,y}^{(2)} \hat G_{n, *}(z_i)\right)^4\right)^{\frac{1}{4}}  \lesssim \left(S^{(z_i)}\right)^{1/4}\left(e^{-r^{(z_i)}(x,y)} + e^{-r^{(z_i)}(y,x)} + q^{(z_i)}(x,y)\right)^\tau \, |W_n|^{-1/2}.
$$
A similar argument also immediately yields that 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:QD}
\left(\mathbb{E}\left(D_x \hat G_{n, *}(z_i)\right)^4\right)^{\frac{1}{4}} \leqslant \left(\mathbb{E}\left|D_x \hat G_{n, *}(z_i)\right|^{4+p/2}\right)^{\frac{1}{4+p/2}} \lesssim \left(S^{(z_i)}\right)^{1/4} |W_n|^{-1/2}.
\end{equation}
Since in both our examples, $S^{(z_i)}(x) \asymp S(x) = 1+ |h|^{5d/2}$ for all $i \in [m]$ and $x=(v,h)$, we use the simple bound $2(S^{(z_i)})^{1/4}(S^{(z_j)})^{1/4} \asymp S^{1/2} \leqslant S^{(z_i)} + S^{(z_j)} \leqslant S$. Plugging these bounds into \eqref{eq:zetas_mult_2} and \eqref{eq:zetas_mult_3}, and dropping the probability factor in \eqref{eq:D2_basic_bound} in one of the integrands in $\zeta_2^{(2)}$, we thus obtain
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:zeta23bd}
		\max\{\zeta_2^{(2)}, \zeta_3^{(2)}\}^2 \lesssim m^3 \sum_{i=1}^m \frac{\mathbb Q f_{\tau,i}^2}{|W_n|^2}.
	\end{equation}
	
	Finally, we bound $\zeta_4^{(2)}$. As argued in the proof of \cite[Lemma 5.7]{BM22}, one has
	$$
	\mathbb P \left(D_{x} \hat G_{n, *}(z_i) \neq 0\right) \leqslant \kappa^{(z_i)}(x) + g^{(z_i)}(x). 
	$$
	Thus, H\"{o}lder's inequality and \eqref{eq:QD} again yield
	\begin{align*}
		\mathbb{E}\left|D_x \hat G_{n, *}(z_i)\right|^3 & \lesssim \left(\mathbb{E}\left|D_x \hat G_{n, *}(z_i)\right|^{4+p/2}\right)^{\frac{3}{4+p/2}} \mathbb P \left(D_x\hat G_{n, *}(z_i) \neq 0\right)^{\frac{2+p}{8+p}}\\
		& \leqslant \left(\mathbb{E}\left|D_x \hat G_{n, *}(z_i)\right|^{4+p/2}\right)^{\frac{3}{4+p/2}} \mathbb P \left(D_x\hat G_{n, *}(z_i) \neq 0\right)^{4\tau}\\
		& \lesssim |W_n|^{-3/2} \left(S^{(z_i)}\right)^{3/4} \left((\kappa^{(z_i)}(x))^{4\tau} + (g^{(z_i)}(x))^{4\tau}\right).
	\end{align*}
	Plugging this bound into \eqref{eq:zetas_mult_4} and dropping the probability factor above in one factor in the integrand in $\zeta_4^{(2)}$, we obtain
$$
\zeta_4^{(2)} \asymp m \sum_{i,j=1}^m \frac{\mathbb Q \left((\kappa^{(z_i)} + g^{(z_i)})^{4\tau} S\right)}{|W_n|^{3/2}}.
$$

A similar bound holds in the volume-weighted case, with the functions $f, \kappa, g$ modified accordingly. Next we bound the specific integrals appearing in the terms $\zeta_1, \zeta_2^{(2)}, \zeta_3^{(2)}$ and $\zeta_4^{(2)}$ separately for the unweighted and the volume-weighted cases.

\smallskip

\noindent \underline{\em Unweighted case.} We can now evaluate these terms as in Section \ref{sec:univ_proof}. First, for each $i \in [m]$, the integral $\mathbb Q f_{\tau,i}^2$ can be bounded in exactly the same manner as in the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:fmombd} in Appendix \ref{apx:univ} via \eqref{eq:f12}, \eqref{eq:f22} and \eqref{eq:f32}, by replacing $z$ by $z_i \in [a,b]$ therein, thus making all constants dependent only on $a,b$. Thus, assuming $\mathbb E H_-^{3d}<\infty$, and arguing exactly the same way as in Section \ref{sec:univ_proof}, we obtain
$$
\mathbb Q f_{\tau,i}^2 =O( |W_n|), \quad i \in [m],
$$
with the constant depending on $a,b$. This yields $\zeta_2^{(2)}, \zeta_3^{(2)} \lesssim m^2 |W_n|^{-1/2}$. Arguing similarly for $\zeta_4^{(2)}$ using \eqref{eq:kappabd} and \eqref{eq:gbd}, assuming $\mathbb E H_-^{3d}<\infty$, one obtains $\zeta_4^{(2)} \lesssim m^3 |W_n|^{-1/2}$. 

Finally, let \(\Sigma= \Sigma(\boldsymbol{z}) =(k(z_i,z_j))_{i,j \in [m]}\), which is a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix. Then, by Theorem \ref{thm:var}, we immediately have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:zeta1_mult}
\zeta_1
=
\sum_{i,j=1}^m
\left|
k(z_i,z_j)
-
\mathsf{Cov}\big(\hat G_{n,*}(z_i),\hat G_{n,*}(z_j)\big)
\right|
=
\sum_{i,j=1}^m
\left|
k(z_i,z_j)
-
\frac{\mathsf{Cov}\big(G_n(z_i),G_n(z_j)\big)}{|W_n|}
\right| = O(|W_n|^{-1/d}).
\end{equation}

\noindent \underline{\em Volume-weighted case.}
By our assumption, $\mathbb E H_-^{m_0d}<\infty$ with $m_0 >5.5$. Also, we take $p=12$ and consequently $\tau=3/20$. Lemma \ref{lem:fmombdV} then yields $
\mathbb Q f_{\tau,i}^2 \lesssim |W_n|
$. Similarly, applying the bound in \eqref{eq:gbdV} and the subsequent estimate corresponding to $\kappa^{(z,\mathsf V)}$ (noting that the bounds also hold with the exponent $4\tau$), we obtain $\mathbb Q \left((\kappa^{(z_i,\mathsf V)} + g^{(z_i,\mathsf V)})^{4\tau} S\right) \lesssim |W_n|$. Thus, we have $\zeta_2^{(2)}, \zeta_3^{(2)} \lesssim m^2 |W_n|^{-1/2}$ while $\zeta_4^{(2)} \lesssim m^3 |W_n|^{-1/2}$.

Finally, let $\Sigma^{\mathsf V}=\Sigma^{\mathsf V}(\boldsymbol{z})
=(k^{\mathsf V}(z_i,z_j))_{i,j\in[m]}$.
Arguing as in \eqref{eq:zeta1_mult} and applying
Theorem \ref{thm:var}, we obtain
\begin{equation*}
\zeta_1
=
\sum_{i,j=1}^m
\left|
k^{\mathsf V}(z_i,z_j)
-
\mathsf{Cov}\big(\hat G^{\mathsf V}_{n,*}(z_i),\hat G^{\mathsf V}_{n,*}(z_j)\big)
\right|
=
\sum_{i,j=1}^m
\left|
k^{\mathsf V}(z_i,z_j)
-
\frac{\mathsf{Cov}\big(G^{\mathsf V}_n(z_i),G^{\mathsf V}_n(z_j)\big)}{|W_n|}
\right| = O(|W_n|^{-1/d}).
\end{equation*}
Since $m$ is fixed, this completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- lemma-27: body_md -->
\label{lem:det-local-extreme}
Let \(J=[a,b]\subset\mathbb R\), put
\(
 R_0:=\frac{\sqrt d}{2},
	\)
	and
	\(
 K_J:=[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]^d\times J,
\)
and define
\[
 A^{(b)}:=
 \left\{(v',h')\in\mathbb X:
 (\|v'\|-R_0)_+^2+h'\leqslant b\right\}.
\]
For every locally finite configuration \(\mu\) and every
\(y=(v,h)\in\mu|_{K_J}\), membership of \(y\) in
\(\mathcal E(\mu)\) is determined by \(\mu|_{A^{(b)}}\).
<!-- end lemma-27 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
Let \(y=(v,h)\in K_J\). If \(x'=(v',h')\) satisfies
\(L(x',v)<L(y,v)=h\), then
\(
 \|v'-v\|^2+h'<h\leqslant b.
\)
Since \(\|v\|\leqslant R_0\), we have
\(
 (\|v'\|-R_0)_+\leqslant\|v'-v\|.
\)
Consequently,
\(
 (\|v'\|-R_0)_+^2+h'<b,
\)
so \(x'\in A^{(b)}\). Thus, every point capable of destroying the
extremality of \(y\) belongs to \(A^{(b)}\).
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- lemma-28: body_md -->
\label{lem:det-ext-overlap}
Assume \(\mathbb E[H_-^{3d}]<\infty\). Let \(A_i^{(b)}\) and
\(A_j^{(b)}\) be translates of \(A^{(b)}\) to the centers of unit cubes
\(z_i,z_j\). Then
\[
 \mathbb Q(A_i^{(b)}\cap A_j^{(b)})
 \in O(\|z_i-z_j\|^{-5d}).
\]
The constant may depend on \(J\), but not on \(i,j\).
<!-- end lemma-28 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
By translation invariance, it is enough to consider
\(A^{(b)}\cap(A^{(b)}+(z,0))\). Put
\(
 r:=\|z\|,\) \( R_0:=\frac{\sqrt d}{2},\) \(
 \tau:=(r/2-R_0)_+,\) and \( U:=(b-H)_+.
\)
If \((v,h)\) belongs to the intersection, then
\(\max\{\|v\|,\|v-z\|\}\geqslant r/2\), and therefore
\(h\leqslant b-\tau^2\), equivalently \(U\geqslant\tau^2\). For fixed \(h\), the
spatial section of the intersection is contained in a ball of radius
\(R_0+\sqrt{(b-h)_+}\). Hence,
\[
 \mathbb Q(A^{(b)}\cap(A^{(b)}+(z,0)))
 \leqslant C\left(
 \mathbb P(U\geqslant\tau^2)
 +\mathbb E[U^{d/2}\mathbf{1}\{U\geqslant\tau^2\}]
 \right).
\]
Since
\(
 \mathbb E[U^{3d}]
 \leqslant C_J\bigl(1+\mathbb E[H_-^{3d}]\bigr)<\infty,
\)
Markov's inequality gives, for \(\tau\geqslant1\) that
\(
 \mathbb P(U\geqslant\tau^2)\leqslant C\tau^{-6d},
	\)
	and
	\(
 \mathbb E[U^{d/2}\mathbf{1}\{U\geqslant\tau^2\}]
 \leqslant \tau^{-5d}\mathbb E[U^{3d}].
\)
The bounded range of \(r\) is absorbed into the constant.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
For the multi-indices in the lemma, put
\[
 \operatorname{dist}(\alpha,\beta):=
 \operatorname{dist}\bigl(
 \{z_{i_a}:1\leqslant a\leqslant r\},
 \{z_{j_b}:1\leqslant b\leqslant s\}
 \bigr).
\]
Let
\[
 A_i^{(b)}:=A^{(b)}+(z_i,0),
 \qquad
 A_\alpha:=\bigcup_{a=1}^rA_{i_a}^{(b)},
 \qquad
 A_\beta:=\bigcup_{b=1}^sA_{j_b}^{(b)}.
\]
Since \(Q_i\times J\subseteq A_i^{(b)}\),
Lemma~\ref{lem:det-local-extreme} shows that \(\Delta_i\) is measurable
with respect to \(\sigma(\mathcal P|_{A_i^{(b)}})\). Thus, \(X_\alpha\) and
\(X_\beta\) are measurable with respect to the corresponding union regions.

Let \(\mathcal P'\) be an independent copy of \(\mathcal P\), and define
\(
 \mathcal P^\beta
 :=
 \mathcal P|_{(A_\alpha\cap A_\beta)^{\complement}}
 +\mathcal P'|_{A_\alpha\cap A_\beta}.
\)
Let \(X_\beta'\) be the same functional as \(X_\beta\), evaluated at
\(\mathcal P^\beta\). Then, \(X_\beta'\stackrel d=X_\beta\), and
\(X_\beta'\) is independent of \(X_\alpha\). Therefore,
\(
 \mathsf{Cov}(X_\alpha,X_\beta)
 =\mathbb E[X_\alpha(X_\beta-X_\beta')].
\)
For every \(u<\infty\), we have
\(
 \sup_{n,I,i}\|\Delta_i(I)\|_u<\infty,
\)
because
\(
 0\leqslant\Delta_i(I)
 \leqslant\mathcal P((Q_i\cap W_n)\times I),
\)
and the Poisson variable on the right has mean at most \(\mathbb F(J)\leqslant1\).
Consequently, Hölder's inequality gives
\(
 \|X_\alpha\|_p\leqslant
 \prod_{a=1}^r\|\Delta_{i_a}\|_{pr}\leqslant C_p,
 \) and \(
 \|X_\beta\|_p+\|X_\beta'\|_p\leqslant C_p.
\)
Since the two point processes differ only on \(A_\alpha\cap A_\beta\), we have
\(
 \mathbb P(X_\beta\ne X_\beta')
 \leqslant2\mathbb Q(A_\alpha\cap A_\beta).
\)
Moreover,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb Q(A_\alpha\cap A_\beta)
 \leqslant\sum_{a=1}^r\sum_{b=1}^s
 \mathbb Q(A_{i_a}^{(b)}\cap A_{j_b}^{(b)})
 \leqslant C(1+\operatorname{dist}(\alpha,\beta))^{-5d}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hölder's inequality  therefore yields
\(
 |\mathsf{Cov}(X_\alpha,X_\beta)|
 \in O_p((1+\operatorname{dist}(\alpha,\beta))^{-5d(1-2/p)}).
\)
Choose
\(
 p\geqslant{10d}/{2d-1}.
\)
Then, \(5d(1-2/p)\geqslant3d+1\), including when \(d=1\), and hence
\(
 |\mathsf{Cov}(X_\alpha,X_\beta)|
 \leqslant C(1+\operatorname{dist}(\alpha,\beta))^{-3d-1}.
\)
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- lemma-29: body_md -->
\label{lem:Q_intersection_cube_envelopes}
Assume \(\mathbb E[H_-^{d/2}]<\infty\). Then, there are
\(C,c_1,c_2\in(0,\infty)\), depending on \(d,\mathbb F,J\), such that for
\(z,z'\in\mathbb Z^d\), \(T,T'\in\mathbb R\), \(M:=T\vee T'\), and
\(r:=\|z-z'\|\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb Q\bigl(
 \widehat D_{z,J}^V(T)\cap\widehat D_{z',J}^V(T')
 \bigr)
 &\leqslant
 C\bigl(1+(M-a)_+^{d/2}\bigr)
 \mathbf{1}\left\{
 r\leqslant c_1\bigl(1+\sqrt{(M-a)_+}\bigr)
 \right\}\\
 &\quad+
 C\int_{-\infty}^{M-c_2r^2}
 \left(
 1+(M-a)_+^{d/2}+(1+u_-)^{d/2}
 \right)\mathbb F(du).
\end{aligned}
\]
<!-- end lemma-29 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
If \((v,u)\) lies in both envelopes, then
\(
 r
 \leqslant
 \sqrt d
 +\sqrt{(T-a)_+}+\sqrt{(T'-a)_+}
 +\sqrt{(T-u)_+}+\sqrt{(T'-u)_+}.
\)
The section of either envelope at mark \(u\) has volume at most
\(
 O\Big(
 (M-a)_+^{d/2}+(1+u_-)^{d/2}
 \Big).
\)
The case of bounded spatial separation follows by integration over \(u\leqslant M\). In the
complementary case, the preceding distance inequality implies
\(u\leqslant M-r^2/16\) after increasing \(c_1\), which gives the term arising from low marks.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- lemma-30: body_md -->
\label{lem:cube_time_tail_under_E}
Let \(I\subseteq J\), and assume \(\mathbb E[H_-^p]<\infty\).
For \(z\in\mathbb Z^d\), define
\[
 \widetilde T_z
 :=
 \sup\left\{
 T_x:
 x\in\mathcal P|_{Q_z\times I},\
 x\in\mathcal E(\mathcal P)
 \right\}.
\]
Then
\(
 \sup_{z\in\mathbb Z^d}
 \mathbb P(\widetilde T_z-a\geqslant t)
 \leqslant Ct^{-p},
\), \(t\geqslant1\).
<!-- end lemma-30 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->
By the union bound and Mecke's formula,
\(
 \mathbb P(\widetilde T_z-a\geqslant t)
 \leqslant
 \int_I
 \mathbb P\bigl(
 (0,h)\in\mathcal E(\mathcal P+\delta_{(0,h)}),\
 T_{(0,h)}-a\geqslant t
 \bigr)\mathbb F(dh).
\)
Since \(h\in J\), we have
	\((T_{(0,h)}-h)_+\geqslant t-(b-a)\) whenever
\(
 T_{(0,h)}-a\geqslant t.
\)
For sufficiently large \(t\), Markov's inequality and
Corollary~\ref{lem:cover-time-moment-integrability} yield \(Ct^{-p}\), uniformly in
\(h\in J\). The bounded range of \(t\) is absorbed into the constant.
<!-- end proof-53 -->
<!-- lemma-31: body_md -->
\label{lem:weighted-inserted-palm-moment}
For every \(\gamma>0\),
\[
 \sup_{x=(v,h):\,h\in J}
 \mathbb E\left[
 \mathbf{1}\{x\in\mathcal E(\mathcal P+\delta_x)\}
 \bigl(1+((b\vee T(x;\mathcal P+\delta_x))-a)_+\bigr)^\gamma
 \right]<\infty.
\]
<!-- end lemma-31 -->
<!-- proof-54: body_md -->
On the extremality event, \(T(x;\mathcal P+\delta_x)\geqslant h\), and, since
\(h\in[a,b]\),
\[
 1+((b\vee T(x;\mathcal P+\delta_x))-a)_+
 \leqslant C_J\bigl(1+(T(x;\mathcal P+\delta_x)-h)_+\bigr).
\]
The assertion now follows from
Corollary~\ref{lem:cover-time-moment-integrability}, applied with upper level
\(b\). Spatial stationarity makes the bound independent of \(v\).
<!-- end proof-54 -->
<!-- lemma-32: body_md -->
\label{lem:weighted-envelope-tail}
Let $\gamma > 3d$ and assume \(\mathbb E[H_-^{3d}]<\infty\). Let \(Z\geqslant0\) and \(S\geqslant a\) be random
variables defined on an auxiliary probability space. If
\[
 \mathbb E\left[Z\bigl(1+(S-a)_+\bigr)^\gamma\right]<\infty,
\]
then, uniformly in \(z\in\mathbb Z^d\),
\[
 \mathbb E\left[
 Z\,\mathbb Q\left(
 \widehat D_{z,J}^V(S)
 \cap\{(v,h):\operatorname{dist}(v,Q_z)>r\}
 \right)
 \right]
 \leqslant
 C(1+r)^{-5d}
 \mathbb E\left[Z\bigl(1+(S-a)_+\bigr)^\gamma\right].
\]
<!-- end lemma-32 -->
<!-- proof-55: body_md -->
Put \(U:=S-a\) and \(R_0:=\sqrt d/2\), and let \(H\sim \mathbb F\) be independent
of \((Z,S)\). For fixed values of \(S\) and \(H\), the spatial section of
\(\widehat D_{z,J}^V(S)\) at mark \(H\) is contained in the ball with center
\(z\) and radius \(R_0+\sqrt U+\sqrt{(S-H)_+}\). Its volume is therefore at
most
\(
 C\bigl(1+U^{d/2}+H_-^{d/2}\bigr),
\)
where the constant depends only on \(J\) and \(d\). If this section contains a
point at distance more than \(r\) from \(Q_z\), then
\(r-R_0<\sqrt U+\sqrt{(S-H)_+}\). For all sufficiently large \(r\), this
implies
\(
 U\geqslant \frac{r^2}{16}
 \;\text{ or }\;
 H_-\geqslant c r^2
\)
for a constant \(c>0\). Indeed, if \(U<r^2/16\), then
\(\sqrt{(S-H)_+}>r/2\); since \(S=a+U<a+r^2/16\), this forces
\(H<a-3r^2/16\), and hence \(H_-\geqslant cr^2\) for large \(r\).
Representing the \(\mathbb Q\)-measure by integration over the independent mark
\(H\), the expectation in the statement is at most a constant times
\(
 \mathbb E\left[Z(1+U^{d/2}+H_-^{d/2})
 \mathbf{1}\left\{U\geqslant\frac{r^2}{16}\text{ or }H_-\geqslant cr^2\right\}\right].
\)
For the event involving \(U\), independence of \(H\) and Markov's inequality
give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E\big[Z(1+U^{d/2}+H_-^{d/2})
 \mathbf{1}\big\{U\geqslant\frac{r^2}{16}\big\}\big]
 \leqslant
 C r^{-2(\gamma-d/2)}
 \mathbb E[Z(1+U)^\gamma]\mathbb E[1+H_-^{d/2}]
 \leqslant C r^{-5d}\mathbb E[Z(1+U)^\gamma],
\end{aligned}
\]
because \(\gamma>3d\). For the event involving \(H_-\), independence gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E\left[Z(1+U^{d/2}+H_-^{d/2})\mathbf{1}\{H_-\geqslant cr^2\}\right]
 &\leqslant
 C\mathbb E[Z(1+U)^\gamma]
 \left(\mathbb P(H_-\geqslant cr^2)
 +\mathbb E[H_-^{d/2}\mathbf{1}\{H_-\geqslant cr^2\}]\right)\\
 &\leqslant C r^{-5d}\mathbb E[Z(1+U)^\gamma].
\end{aligned}
\]
The last line follows from \(\mathbb E[H_-^{3d}]<\infty\): the two terms have orders
\(r^{-6d}\) and \(r^{-5d}\), respectively.
<!-- end proof-55 -->
<!-- lemma-33: body_md -->
\label{lem:weighted-deterministic-comparison}
Let \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) be locally finite configurations that agree on
\(S_r(\mathcal A)\), where \(|\mathcal A|\leqslant3\), and assume that each
configuration has finitely many points in every downward paraboloid
\(D(w,t)\). Assume that neither
configuration has a point in
\(\bigcup_{i\in\mathcal A}A_i^{\mathrm{ext}}\setminus S_r(\mathcal A)\).
Assume also that every point
\(x\in\operatorname{supp}(\mu)\cap\operatorname{supp}(\nu)\cap Q_{\mathcal A}^I\) that is extreme in either
configuration has a bounded cell, and hence a finite cover time, in that
configuration. Finally, for each such extreme point, assume that
\[
 \mu\big(D^V(x,T(x;\mu))\setminus S_r(\mathcal A)\big)=0
\]
when \(x\) is extreme in \(\mu\), and impose the analogous condition for
\(\nu\). Then
\(
 \Delta_i^V(I;\mu)=\Delta_i^V(I;\nu),\qquad i\in\mathcal A.
\)
<!-- end lemma-33 -->
<!-- proof-56: body_md -->
Put \(S:=S_r(\mathcal A)\). Since \(Q_{\mathcal A}^I\subseteq S\), the two
configurations have the same candidate generators in the blocks under
consideration. Fix one of them, say \(x=(v,h)\in Q_i^I\). If \(x\) is not extreme in \(\mu\), Lemma~\ref{lem:det-local-extreme} identifies a point
of \(\mu|_{A_i^{\mathrm{ext}}}\) that beats \(x\) at \(v\). By assumption,
this point lies in \(S\), and therefore also belongs to \(\nu\). The converse
argument is identical, so \(x\) has the same extremality status in both
configurations.

Suppose now that \(x\) is extreme in both configurations, and write
\(C_\mu:=C(x;\mu)\), \(C_\nu:=C(x;\nu)\), and
\(T_\mu:=T(x;\mu)\), \(T_\nu:=T(x;\nu)\). These cells are bounded by
assumption. We prove \(C_\mu\subseteq C_\nu\). If this inclusion fails, choose
\(u\in C_\mu\setminus C_\nu\). Since extremality implies
\(v\in C_\mu\cap C_\nu\), the segment from \(v\) to \(u\) has a first exit
point \(w\) from the closed convex set \(C_\nu\). At that point, one of the
Laguerre halfspaces defining \(C_\nu\) becomes active. Thus, there is a
competitor \(y\in\operatorname{supp}(\nu)\setminus\{x\}\) such that
\(
 L(y,w)=L(x,w)\leqslant T_\nu,
\)
and immediately beyond \(w\) toward \(u\), one has \(L(y,\cdot)<L(x,\cdot)\).
If \(y\in S\), then \(y\in\mu\). Points of the segment immediately
beyond \(w\) belong to \(C_\mu\) by convexity, but they are beaten by
\(y\), a contradiction. Hence, \(y\notin S\). Writing \(y=(w_y,s_y)\), the equality at
\(w\) and the bound \(L(x,w)\leqslant T_\nu\) give
\[
 s_y\leqslant T_\nu,
	\text{ and }
 \|w_y-v\|\leqslant
 \sqrt{(T_\nu-s_y)_+}+\sqrt{(T_\nu-h)_+}.
\]
Therefore, \(y\in D^V(x,T_\nu)\setminus S\), contrary to the hypothesis for
\(\nu\). This proves \(C_\mu\subseteq C_\nu\). Interchanging \(\mu\) and
\(\nu\) gives equality. Hence, the cell volumes and all block contributions
coincide.
<!-- end proof-56 -->
<!-- proof-57: body_md -->
Put \(S:=S_r(\mathcal A)\). We first consider the deterministic extremality
regions. If a point belongs to
\(A_i^{\mathrm{ext}}\setminus S\), then its spatial coordinate is at distance
more than \(r\) from \(Q_i\). The definition of
\(A_i^{\mathrm{ext}}\) therefore forces its mark to be at most
\(b-c r^2\), after changing \(c>0\) by a constant depending only on \(d\).
As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:det-ext-overlap}, we have
\(
 \mathbb Q(A_i^{\mathrm{ext}}\setminus S)
 \leqslant C\int_{-\infty}^{b-cr^2}
 \bigl(1+(b-h)_+^{d/2}\bigr)\mathbb F(dh)
 \leqslant C(1+r)^{-5d}.
\)
The last estimate uses \(\mathbb E[H_-^{3d}]<\infty\). Since
\(|\mathcal A|\leqslant3\), the first part of the event on which localization fails has probability of the same order.

For the volume part, the union bound by the number of ordered pairs of Poisson
points, followed by the twofold Mecke formula, gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\mathbb P\left(
 \exists x\in\mathcal E(\mathcal P)\cap Q_{\mathcal A}^I:
 \mathcal P(D^V(x,T(x;\mathcal P))\setminus S)>0
 \right)\\
 &\quad\leqslant
 \sum_{i\in\mathcal A}\int_{Q_i^I}
 \mathbb E\left[
 \mathbf{1}\{x\in\mathcal E(\mathcal P+\delta_x)\}
 \mathbb Q\left(
 \widehat D_{i,J}^V(b\vee T(x;\mathcal P+\delta_x))\setminus S
 \right)
 \right]\mathbb Q(dx).
\end{aligned}
\]
Indeed, after inserting both \(x\) and a possible exterior point \(y\),
insertion of \(y\) cannot create extremality of \(x\), and it can only shrink
the cell of \(x\). By the radius representation of the cover time,
\(
 T(x;\mathcal P+\delta_x+\delta_y)\leqslant T(x;\mathcal P+\delta_x).
\)
Lemma~\ref{lem:env} then places the corresponding region that determines the score inside the
envelope in the last display.
For fixed \(x\in Q_i^I\), apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:weighted-envelope-tail} with
\(
 Z:=\mathbf{1}\{x\in\mathcal E(\mathcal P+\delta_x)\},
 \) and \(
 S_x:=b\vee T(x;\mathcal P+\delta_x).
\)
The required weighted moment is supplied by
Lemma~\ref{lem:weighted-inserted-palm-moment}. Since a point outside
\(S_r(\mathcal A)\) is at distance more than \(r\) from \(Q_i\), the lemma
gives, uniformly in \(x\in Q_i^I\), that
\(
 \mathbb E\left[
 Z\,\mathbb Q\left(\widehat D_{i,J}^V(S_x)\setminus S\right)
 \right]
 \leqslant C(1+r)^{-5d}.
\)
Finally, \(\mathbb Q(Q_i^I)\leqslant\mathbb F(I)\leqslant1\). Combining the extremality and volume estimates proves
the claim.
<!-- end proof-57 -->
<!-- proof-58: body_md -->
Put \(S:=S_r(\mathcal A)\) and
\(\mathcal F:=\sigma(\mathcal P|_S)\). Let \(\mathcal P'\) be an independent copy of
\(\mathcal P\), and define
\(
 \mathcal P^*:=\mathcal P|_S+\mathcal P'|_{S^{\complement}}.
\)
Conditionally on \(\mathcal F\), the restrictions of \(\mathcal P\) and \(\mathcal P^*\)
to \(S^{\complement}\) are independent Poisson processes with the same
intensity. Thus, if \(X_{\mathcal A}^*\) denotes the same centered block
product evaluated at \(\mathcal P^*\), then
\(\mathbb E[X_{\mathcal A}^*\mid\mathcal F]
 =\mathbb E[X_{\mathcal A}\mid\mathcal F]=X_{\mathcal A}^{(r)}\). Conditioning
first on \(\mathcal P\) and applying Jensen's inequality gives
\(
 \|X_{\mathcal A}-X_{\mathcal A}^{(r)}\|_{a_0}
 \leqslant \|X_{\mathcal A}-X_{\mathcal A}^*\|_{a_0}.
\)
The processes \(\mathcal P\) and \(\mathcal P^*\) agree on \(S\), and both have bounded
Laguerre cells almost surely because \(\mathcal P^*\) has the same law as \(\mathcal P\).
On the complement of \(\mathsf B_{\mathcal A}(r;\mathcal P)\cup
\mathsf B_{\mathcal A}(r;\mathcal P^*)\), the remaining hypotheses of
Lemma~\ref{lem:weighted-deterministic-comparison} hold, and hence
\(X_{\mathcal A}=X_{\mathcal A}^*\). Put
\(
 E_r:=\mathsf B_{\mathcal A}(r;\mathcal P)
 \cup\mathsf B_{\mathcal A}(r;\mathcal P^*).
\)
For the fixed exponents \(1<a_0<p\), H\"older's inequality gives
\(
 \|X_{\mathcal A}-X_{\mathcal A}^*\|_{a_0}
 \leqslant
 \|X_{\mathcal A}-X_{\mathcal A}^*\|_p
 \mathbb P(E_r)^{1/a_0-1/p}
 \leqslant C\mathbb P(E_r)^{1/a_0-1/p}.
\)
The last inequality follows from
Lemma~\ref{lem:weighted-block-product-moments} and the fact that
\(\mathcal P^*\) has the same law as \(\mathcal P\). Lemma~\ref{lem:weighted-bad-event}
therefore yields
\(
 \|X_{\mathcal A}-X_{\mathcal A}^{(r)}\|_{a_0}
 \leqslant C(1+r)^{-5d(1/a_0-1/p)}
	\in O(r^{-3d-1}).
\)
<!-- end proof-58 -->
